In the Name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Surat Al 'Imran

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And none knows its interpretation except Allah﴾. It is possible that what is meant by *ta'wil* (interpretation, here meaning the ultimate reality of a matter) in this noble verse is *tafsir* (explanation) and comprehension of the meaning. It is also possible that what is meant by it is the true reality of the matter to which it returns. We have already mentioned in the introduction to this book that among the types of clarification we noted is that when one of the two possibilities is the predominant one in the Qur'an, this indicates that the predominant possibility is what is intended, because interpreting according to the more frequent usage takes precedence over interpreting according to other usages. Once you know this, be aware that the predominant usage of *ta'wil* in the Qur'an is its application to the true reality of the matter to which it returns, such as:

• His saying: ﴿This is the interpretation of my dream from before﴾ [Yusuf: 100],
• His saying: ﴿Do they await anything but its interpretation? The day its interpretation comes﴾ [Yunus: 39],
• His saying: ﴿Rather, they denied that which they did not encompass in knowledge, and its interpretation had not yet come to them﴾ [Yunus: 39],
• His saying: ﴿That is better and more excellent in outcome (ta'wilan)﴾ [al-Nisa': 59],

along with other verses. Ibn Jarir al-Tabari said: The origin of *ta'wil* is from *ala al-shay'u ila kadha* (the thing returned to such-and-such) when it arrives at it and returns to it, or does not. And *awwaltuhu* means I caused it to return to it. He said: Some transmitters have recited the verse of al-A'sha:

*[Tawil meter]*
"Because her love was, as it were, returning (ta'awwul) to its end, like the return of a young camel's colt that has been led to submission."

He said: By his saying *ta'awwul hubbiha* he means the end and the return of her love. He only means by this that her love was small in his heart, then it grew from smallness to greatness, continuing to grow until it became submissive, just as a young camel colt that continues to grow until it becomes submissive and becomes large like its mother. He said: This verse is sometimes recited as:

*[Tawil meter]*
"Because her affections were the followers of her love, following the return of a young camel's colt until it became submissive."

End quote. Accordingly, there is no evidence in it. *Al-Ribi'* is the colt born at the beginning of the birthing season, and *asḥaba* means to submit to whoever leads it. From it is the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

*[Mutaqarib meter]*
"I am not one with weak joints, submissive, who, when forced into restraint, becomes obedient."

[p. 190] *Al-ratyah* is pain in the joints, and *al-immar* (with a kasra on the hamza and a shadda on the mim, fatha after it, followed by a ra') is one who obeys everyone because of his weakness. Al-Azhari and the author of *Lisan al-'Arab* recited the aforementioned verse of al-A'sha as:

*[Tawil meter]*
"But she was the spoiled one of her two cousins, following the return of a young camel's colt until it became submissive."

They elaborated on its explanation, and in this version too there is no evidence.

Note:
Know that *ta'wil* is used in three senses:

The first: it is what we have mentioned, namely the reality to which the matter returns, and this is its meaning in the Qur'an.

The second: it is used to mean *tafsir* (explanation) and *bayan* (clarification). From this meaning is his saying (ﷺ) about Ibn 'Abbas: "O Allah, grant him understanding in the religion and teach him *ta'wil*." Also the saying of Ibn Jarir and other scholars: "The discussion concerning the *ta'wil* of His saying, may He be exalted, such-and-such," meaning its *tafsir* and clarification. And the saying of 'A'ishah, which is authentically established in the Sahih: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to frequently say in his bowing and prostration: 'Glory be to You, O Allah, our Lord, and praise be to You. O Allah, forgive me'" — *yata'awwalu al-Qur'an*, meaning he acts upon it and implements it. And Allah knows best.

The third: this is its meaning as commonly used in the terminology of the usulis (jurists of legal theory), which is diverting a word from its apparent, immediately understood meaning to a weaker possibility, by means of an indicator that points to that. The summary of the discussion of *ta'wil* according to the usulis is that it cannot be free of one of three states, by correct division:

The first: that the diversion of a word from its apparent meaning is based on a sound proof in reality that indicates this. This is what they call the *ta'wil sahih* (correct interpretation) and *ta'wil qarib* (near interpretation), such as his saying (ﷺ), authentically established in the Sahih: "The neighbor has more right to his *saqb* (adjacent property)." Its apparent, immediately understood meaning is that the right of pre-emptive purchase (*shufah*) belongs to the neighbor. Restricting "neighbor" in this hadith to specifically a partner who shares undivided property is restricting it to a weaker possibility, but the authentic hadith indicates this, explicitly stating that when the paths are distinguished and the boundaries are set, there is no *shufah*.

The second state: the diversion of a word from its apparent meaning is for a reason that the one diverting believes to be a proof but is not a proof in reality. This is what they call the *ta'wil fasid* (corrupt interpretation) and *ta'wil ba'id* (remote interpretation). The Shafi'is, Malikis, and Hanbalis gave as an example Imam Abu Hanifa's (may Allah have mercy on him) interpretation of "woman" in his (ﷺ) saying: "Any woman who marries without the permission of her guardian, her marriage is void, void," as referring to a *mukatabah* (a slave woman contracted for manumission) and a young girl. And also his (may Allah have mercy on him) interpretation of "poor man" in the phrase "sixty poor men" as referring to the *mudd* (a unit of measure), so that he permitted giving sixty *mudd*s to one poor man.

The third state: the diversion of a word from its apparent meaning without any proof at all. In the terminology of the usulis this is called *la'ib* (playful, frivolous interpretation), like the saying of some Shi'ah: ﴿Indeed, Allah commands you to slaughter a cow﴾ [al-Baqarah: 67], meaning 'A'ishah (may Allah be pleased with her).

In *Maraqi al-Su'ud* (a versified work on legal theory) he pointed to the definition of *ta'wil* and the explanation of the three categories with his saying, defining *ta'wil*:

*[Rajaz meter]*
"Interpreting an apparent meaning as a weaker one, and divide it into the corrupt and the sound."

"Its sound form is the near one that is carried, with the strength of the proof in the eyes of the one who derives it."

"Its other form is the corrupt and the remote, and what lies outside these is frivolous."

Then he said:

*[Rajaz meter]*
"Making 'poor man' mean the *mudd* carries clear signs of remoteness."

"Like carrying 'woman' to mean the young girl, and what contradicts the free adult woman."

"And carrying what came concerning fasting to mean making up (qada') with the obligation."

As for *ta'wil* in the terminology of Khalil ibn Ishaq al-Maliki, specific to him in his *Mukhtasar* (abridgment), it refers to the differences among the commentaries on the *Mudawwanah* regarding what is meant by Malik (may Allah have mercy on him). He indicated this in *Maraqi* with his saying:

*[Rajaz meter]*
"And the disagreement in understanding the Book made it a *ta'wil* in the view of the *Mukhtasar*."

In the terminology of the Maliki jurists, "the Book" is the *Mudawwanah*.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And those firmly grounded in knowledge say: We believe in it﴾, the verse [Al 'Imran: 7]. It is not hidden that this *waw* (and) may be resumptive, so that His saying ﴿and those firmly grounded in knowledge﴾ is a subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is *yaqulun* (they say). On this reading, the ambiguous (mutashabih) verses are known only to Allah alone, and the pause on the word "Allah" is complete. It is also possible that the *waw* is coordinating (ʿatif), so that ﴿and those firmly grounded﴾ is conjoined to the word "Allah." On this reading, the ambiguous verses are known in their interpretation by ﴿those firmly grounded in knowledge﴾ as well. And there are indications in the verse showing that the *waw* is resumptive, not coordinating.

Ibn Qudamah said in *Rawdat al-Nazir* the following text: "Because in the verse there are indicators that show that Allah, glory be to Him, alone has knowledge of the ambiguous, and that the correct pause is at His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And none knows its interpretation except Allah﴾, both verbally and in meaning. As for the wording: if He had intended to coordinate those firmly grounded, He would have said *wa-yaqulun amanna bihi* with a *waw*. As for the meaning: because it is a condemnation of those who seek interpretation, and if that knowledge were known to those firmly grounded, then one who seeks it would be praised, not blamed. Also, because their saying *amanna bihi* indicates a kind of entrusting and submission to something whose meaning they have not grasped, especially when they follow it with their saying: ﴿Each is from our Lord﴾. Their mention of their Lord here gives confidence in Him and submission to His command, and that it came from Him, just as the clear (muhkam) verses came from Him. And because the particle *amma* is used to divide sentences, and its mention in ﴿As for those in whose hearts is deviation﴾, together with His description of them as following the ambiguous and seeking its interpretation, indicates another category that differs from them in this attribute, namely those firmly grounded. If they knew its interpretation, they would not have opposed the first category in seeking interpretation. And since it has been established that its interpretation is not known to anyone, it is not permissible to interpret it other than as we have mentioned." End quote from *al-Rawdah*, in its wording.

And among what supports that the *waw* is resumptive, not coordinating, is the inductive evidence in the Qur'an: whenever He, may He be exalted, negates something from creation and affirms it for Himself, no partner shares with Him in that affirmation, such as:

• His saying: ﴿Say: None in the heavens and the earth knows the unseen except Allah﴾ [al-Naml: 65],
• His saying: ﴿None will reveal it at its time except Him﴾ [al-A'raf: 187],
• His saying: ﴿Everything will perish except His Face﴾ [al-Qasas: 88].

So what conforms to this is that His saying ﴿And none knows its interpretation except Allah﴾ means that none knows it except Him alone, as al-Khattabi said. He said: "If the *waw* in His saying ﴿and those firmly grounded in knowledge﴾ were a coordinating *waw*, then His saying ﴿Each is from our Lord﴾ would serve no purpose." The view that the pause is complete at His saying "except Allah," and that His saying "and those firmly grounded" begins a new statement, is the view of the majority of scholars, due to the Qur'anic evidence we have cited.

Among those who held this view were 'Umar, Ibn 'Abbas, 'A'ishah, 'Urwah ibn al-Zubayr, 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz, Ibn Mas'ud, and Ubayy ibn Ka'b. Al-Qurtubi and others reported this from them. Ibn Jarir reported it from Yunus, from Ashhab, from Malik ibn Anas, and it is the position of al-Kisa'i, al-Akhfash, al-Farra', and Abu 'Ubayd.

Abu Nahik al-Asadi said: "You join this verse, but it is a separate statement, and the knowledge of those firmly grounded only reaches to their saying: ﴿We believe in it; each is from our Lord﴾."

The view that the *waw* is coordinating is also reported from Ibn 'Abbas, and Mujahid, al-Rabi', Muhammad ibn Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr, al-Qasim ibn Muhammad, and others held it. Among those who defended this view and elaborated on it was Ibn Fawrak. A parallel to the verse in admitting both the resumptive and coordinating readings is the poet's verse:

*[Murraf al-Kamil meter]*
"The wind weeps with its sorrow, and the lightning flashes in the cloud."

It is possible that "and the lightning" is a subject, with the predicate "flashes" as in the first interpretation, so that it is separate from what precedes it. It is also possible that it is coordinated with "the wind," and "flashes" is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) in the second interpretation, meaning "flashing."

Those who held that the *waw* is coordinating argued that Allah, glory be to Him and exalted, praised them for being firmly grounded in knowledge, so how could He praise them for that if they were ignorant?

Al-Qurtubi said: "Our shaykh Abu al-'Abbas Ahmad ibn 'Amr said: This view is the correct one, for calling them 'firmly grounded' implies that they know more than the clear verses, whose knowledge is shared by everyone who understands the speech of the Arabs. And in what would their firm grounding consist if they knew only what everyone knows?" End quote in its wording.

The annotator of this work, may Allah pardon him, says: The reply to the statement of the aforementioned shaykh of al-Qurtubi is that their firm grounding in knowledge is the very reason that made them stop where their knowledge ends, and say concerning what they have not grasped the true knowledge of, from the speech of Allah, may He be majestic and exalted: ﴿We believe in it; each is from our Lord﴾. This is unlike those who are not firmly grounded, who follow ﴿what is ambiguous of it, seeking discord and seeking its interpretation﴾. This is evident.

Among those who said the *waw* is coordinating is al-Zamakhshari in his *tafsir*, *al-Kashshaf*. And Allah knows best, and attributing knowledge to Him is safest.

Some scholars said: The verification in this matter is that those who said it is coordinating understood *ta'wil* to mean *tafsir* and comprehension of meaning, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "O Allah, teach him *ta'wil*," meaning the explanation and understanding of the meanings of the Qur'an. Those firmly grounded understand what they were addressed with, even if they do not encompass knowledge of the realities of things in their full nature. And those who said it is resumptive understood *ta'wil* to mean the true reality to which the matter returns, and this is known only to Allah. This is a fine distinction, but two issues arise for it:

**The first:** the saying of Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him: "Tafsir (interpretation) is of four kinds: an interpretation that no one is excused for not understanding; an interpretation that the Arabs know from their languages; an interpretation that the scholars know; and an interpretation that none knows but Allah." This is an explicit statement from Ibn 'Abbas that what none knows but Allah is the meaning of tafsir, not what the reality of the matter ultimately comes to.

His saying contradicts the detail mentioned above.

**The second:** the disjointed letters (al-huruf al-muqatta'ah) at the beginnings of the surahs, no one knows their intended meaning but Allah, since no evidence has been established that any specific meaning is what is intended by them, from the Book, the Sunnah, or the consensus (ijma', scholarly agreement), or from the language of the Arabs. So asserting definitively that their meaning is such-and-such is arbitrary judgment without evidence.

**Two notes**

**The first:** Know that, on the view that the waw (و) is conjunctive (ʿatifah), the i'rab (grammatical analysis) of the clause "yaqulūna" (يَقُولُونَ, "they say") is problematic from three aspects:

The first is that it is a ḥāl (circumstantial clause) relating to the conjoined element, which is "al-rāsikhūn" (الرَّاسِخُونَ, "those firmly rooted"), and not to the element it is conjoined to, which is the word of majesty (lafẓ al-jalālah, i.e. Allah). What is well known is that a ḥāl comes either from the conjoined element or from the element it is conjoined to together, as in your saying: "Zayd and ʿAmr came riding (rākibayn)."

And the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And He subjected for you the sun and the moon, both constant (dāʾibayn)﴾ [Ibrahim: 33].

This objection falls away, because it is permissible for a ḥāl to come from the conjoined element alone, not from the element it is conjoined to. Among its examples in the Qur'an is the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And your Lord comes, and the angels, rank upon rank (ṣaffan ṣaffan)﴾ [al-Fajr: 22]. Here "ṣaffan" is a ḥāl from the conjoined element, which is "al-malak" (the angels), and not from the element it is conjoined to, which is the word "rabbuka" (your Lord). And the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And those who came after them say: "Our Lord, forgive us..."﴾ (the verse) [al-Ḥashr: 10]. Here the clause "yaqulūna" is a ḥāl from the waw of the subject in His saying "alladhīna jāʾū" (those who came), and that is conjoined to His saying: ﴿for the poor emigrants﴾ [al-Ḥashr: 8], and His saying: ﴿and those who settled in the abode and the faith﴾ [al-Ḥashr: 9]. So it is a ḥāl from the conjoined element and not from the element it is conjoined to, as Ibn Kathir and others have explained.

The second aspect of the mentioned problems is what al-Qurtubi related from al-Khattabi. He said about him: "Some people of the language argued for it, saying its meaning is: 'and those firmly rooted in knowledge know it, saying: "We believe".' He claimed that the position of 'yaqulūna' is in the accusative as a ḥāl. The majority of the people of the language reject this and consider it unlikely, because the Arabs do not omit both the verb and the object together, and they do not mention a ḥāl except when the verb is apparent. If no verb appears, there is no ḥāl. If that were permissible, it would be permissible to say: 'ʿAbdullah rākiban' meaning: 'ʿAbdullah came riding.' It is only permissible with the verb mentioned, like His saying: 'ʿAbdullah yatakallamu yuṣliḥu bayn al-nās' (ʿAbdullah speaks, reconciling between people), so 'yuṣliḥu' is a ḥāl for him, like the saying of the poet, which Abu ʿUmar recited to me, saying: Abu al-ʿAbbas Thaʿlab recited to us:"

[Rajaz]
"I sent into it a shegaṭ-camel, short-legged (qaṭiman lukālikan),
it shortens (its stride), walking, and lengthens while kneeling (bārikan)"

Meaning: it shortens its stride while walking.

This objection too falls away, because the verb operating in the mentioned ḥāl is not omitted, since it is mentioned in His saying "yaʿlamu" (knows). But the ḥāl comes from the conjoined element and not from the element it is conjoined to, as al-ʿAllamah al-Shawkani explained in his *Tafsir*, and this is clear.

The third aspect of the mentioned problems is: the known principle in the Arabic language is that the ḥāl is a qualifier (qayd) of its operating verb and a description (waṣf) of its owner. So it is problematic to restrict this operating verb, which is "yaʿlamu" (knows), by this ḥāl, which is "yaqūlūna āmannā" (they say: we believed). For there is no basis for restricting the knowledge of those firmly rooted by their saying "āmannā bihi" (we believed in it), because its implication would be that when they do not say "āmannā bihi," they do not know its interpretation, and this is false. This objection is strong, and it indicates the prohibition of the circumstantial sense in the clause "yaqulūna" on the view of conjunction.

**The second note:** If the clause "yaqulūna" cannot be a ḥāl for what we mentioned, what then is its i'rab on the view that the waw is conjunctive? The answer, and Allah knows best: it is conjoined by a deleted particle, and conjunction by a deleted particle has been permitted by Ibn Malik and a group of the scholars of Arabic grammar. The correct view is its permissibility, and that it is not restricted to poetic necessity, as some scholars of Arabic grammar claimed. The evidence for its permissibility is its occurrence in the Qur'an and in the speech of the Arabs.

Among its examples in the Qur'an is the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Faces on that day will be joyful﴾ (the verse) [al-Ghashiyah: 8]. It is undoubtedly conjoined to His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Faces on that day will be humbled﴾ [al-Ghashiyah: 2], by a deleted particle, which is the waw. And the evidence for it is the affirmation of the waw in its counterpart in His saying, the Exalted, in the surah "al-Qiyamah": ﴿Faces on that day radiant﴾ ﴿looking toward their Lord﴾ ﴿And faces on that day frowning﴾ (the verse) [al-Qiyamah: 22–24]. And His saying, the Exalted, in "ʿAbasa": ﴿Faces on that day bright﴾ ﴿laughing, rejoicing﴾ ﴿And faces on that day upon them is dust﴾ (the verse) [ʿAbasa: 38–40].

Some scholars counted among it His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Nor (is there blame) upon those who came to you that you might carry them, (and) you said﴾ (the verse) [al-Tawbah: 92]. He said: meaning "wa-qult" (and you said), by conjunction with a deleted waw. This is one of the possibilities mentioned by Ibn Hisham in *al-Mughni*. Some also counted among it: ﴿Indeed, the religion with Allah is Islam﴾ [Al ʿImran: 19], according to the reading that opens the hamza of "inna." He said: it is conjoined by a deleted particle to His saying: ﴿Allah bears witness that there is no deity except Him﴾ [Al ʿImran: 18], meaning: "and He bore witness that the religion with Allah is Islam." This is also one of the possibilities mentioned by the author of *al-Mughni*. Among it is the ḥadith: "A man gave in charity from his dinar, from his dirham, from a ṣāʿ of his wheat, from a ṣāʿ of his dates," meaning: "and from his dirham, and from a ṣāʿ..." etc.

This was related by al-Ashmuni and others. The ḥadith mentioned was recorded by Muslim, Imam Ahmad, and the authors of the Sunan.

From the evidences for the deletion of the conjunctive particle is the saying of the poet:

[Khafif]
"How did you rise, how did you spend the evening, from what
plants love in the heart of the noble"

Meaning: "and how did you spend the evening."

And the saying of al-Ḥuṭayʾah:

[Basit]
"Indeed, a man whose kin are in Syria, whose dwelling is
in the sands of Yabrin, is a neighbor, though they have been far apart"

Meaning: "and whose dwelling is in the sands of Yabrin."

It has been said that the second clause is a second qualifier, not a conjoined element, and on this view there is no evidence in the verse. Among those who permitted conjunction by a deleted particle are al-Farisi and Ibn ʿUsfur, in disagreement with Ibn Jinni and al-Suhayli.

There is no doubt that in the Qur'an there are matters that none knows but Allah, such as the reality of the soul, because Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿They ask you about the soul. Say: "The soul is of the command of my Lord"﴾ (the verse) [al-Isra': 85]. And like the keys of the unseen, which He stated none knows but Him, by His saying: ﴿And with Him are the keys of the unseen﴾ (the verse) [al-Anʿam: 59].

It has been established from the Prophet (ﷺ) that they are the five mentioned in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, Allah has knowledge of the Hour, and He sends down the rain﴾ (the verse) [Luqman: 34]. And like the disjointed letters at the beginnings of the surahs, and like the delights of Paradise.

• Due to His saying, the Exalted: ﴿No soul knows what has been hidden for them of comfort for the eyes﴾ (the verse) [al-Sajdah: 17]. And within it are matters that those firmly rooted in knowledge know, apart from others.

• Like His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So by your Lord, We will surely question them all﴾ ﴿about what they used to do﴾ [al-Ḥijr: 92–93].

• And His saying: ﴿So We will surely question those to whom messengers were sent, and We will surely question the messengers﴾ [al-Aʿraf: 6], along with His saying: ﴿So on that day no one will be questioned about his sin, man or jinn﴾ [al-Raḥman: 39].

• And His saying: ﴿And the criminals will not be questioned about their sins﴾ [al-Qasas: 78].

• And like His saying: ﴿and a soul from Him﴾ [al-Nisa': 171].

And "al-rusukh" (الرُّسُوخ) means firmness and stability. From it is the saying of the poet:

[Tawil]
"Indeed, a love for Layla has taken firm root in my heart,
its signs refuse to change"

The author said in (*Daf' Iham al-Idtirab ʿan Ayat al-Kitab*):

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Surat Al ʿImran.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿He it is who sent down to you the Book; in it are verses that are muhkam (clear and definitive), they are the foundation of the Book, and others are mutashabih (allegorical, ambiguous)﴾ (the verse).

This noble verse indicates that in the Qur'an there is the muhkam and in it the mutashabih.

Other verses have come indicating that all of it is muhkam, and a verse indicating that all of it is mutashabih. As for those that indicate its entire muhkam nature, they are His saying, the Exalted: ﴿A Book whose verses have been made firm, then detailed, from One Wise and Acquainted﴾ [Hud: 1]. As for those indicating that all of it is mutashabih, they are His saying, the Exalted: ﴿A Book, mutashabih, oft-repeated﴾ [al-Zumar: 23]. The way to reconcile these verses is that the meaning of its being entirely muhkam is that it is in the utmost firmness, i.e., perfection, in its words, its meanings, and its inimitability; its reports are true, its rulings are just, and no flaw or defect afflicts it, neither in words nor in meanings.

The meaning of its being mutashabih is that its verses resemble one another in excellence, truthfulness, inimitability, and freedom from all defects. The meaning of part of it being muhkam and part of it being mutashabih is that the muhkam part is clear in meaning to everyone, like His saying: ﴿And do not approach fornication﴾ [al-Isra': 32] and ﴿And do not set up with Allah another deity﴾ [al-Isra': 39].

And the mutashabih is what its knowledge is hidden from those other than the firmly rooted in knowledge, based on the premise that the waw in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and those firmly rooted in knowledge﴾ [Al ʿImran: 7] is conjunctive; or it is what Allah has kept the knowledge of, like the meanings of the disjointed letters at the beginnings of the surahs, based on the premise that the waw in His saying: ﴿and those firmly rooted in knowledge﴾ is resumptive (istiʾnafiyyah) and not conjunctive.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 3, verse 10:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve, their wealth and their children will never avail them anything against Allah. And they are the fuel of the Fire.﴾ In this noble verse, He mentioned that the disbelievers on the Day of Resurrection will not be helped at all by their wealth or their children, and He mentioned that they are the fuel of the Fire, i.e., its firewood, by which it is kindled. He did not clarify here whether this negation is a refutation of their claim that their wealth and children would benefit them. However, He clarified in other places that they made this claim out of the assumption that He gave them wealth and children in this world only because of their honor with Him and their deserving of that, and that the Hereafter is like this world, in which they deserve that as well. So He refuted them in many verses. Among the verses indicating that they made this claim is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And they say, "We have more wealth and children, and we will not be punished"﴾ [Saba: 35], and His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Have you seen the one who disbelieved in Our signs?﴾ [Maryam: 77], and He said: ﴿"I will surely be given wealth and children"﴾, meaning in the Hereafter as I was given it in this world. And His saying: ﴿And if I am returned to my Lord, indeed I will have with Him the best [reward]﴾ [Fussilat: 50], i.e., by the evidence of what He gave me in this world. And His saying: ﴿And if I am returned to my Lord, I will surely find better than these as a destination﴾ [al-Kahf: 36], an analogy he made of the Hereafter to this world. Allah refuted this claim of theirs in many verses:

• Such as His saying here: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve, their wealth will never avail them﴾, the verse [Al 'Imran: 116],

• And His saying: ﴿Do they think that what We extend to them of wealth and children [means] ﴿We hasten for them into good things? Rather, they do not perceive﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 55-56],

• And His saying: ﴿And it is not your wealth or your children that bring you nearer to Us in position﴾ [Saba: 37],

• And His saying: ﴿And let not those who disbelieve think that Our giving them respite is good for them. We only give them respite that they may increase in sin, and for them is a humiliating punishment﴾ [Al 'Imran: 178],

• And His saying: ﴿We will lead them step by step from where they do not know. And I will give them respite; indeed, My plan is firm﴾ [al-Qalam: 44-45].

And other verses besides these.

He stated in another place that their being the fuel of the Fire mentioned here is for eternity, and that is His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve, their wealth and their children will never avail them anything against Allah. And they are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein eternally﴾ [Al 'Imran: 116].

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 3, verse 11:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Like the custom of the people of Pharaoh and those before them, who denied Our signs, so Allah seized them for their sins﴾, he did not specify here who those before them were, nor what their sins were for which Allah seized them.

He explained in other places that among them were the people of Noah, the people of Hud, the people of Salih, the people of Lut (p-198) and the people of Shu'ayb; and that the sins for which He seized them were disbelief in Allah, denial of the messengers, and other disobediences, such as the hamstringing of the she-camel by Thamud, the sodomy of the people of Lut, and the cheating of the people of Shu'ayb in measure and weight, and other things, as has come in detail in many verses, such as His saying about Noah and his people: ﴿So he remained among them a thousand years less fifty years, and the flood seized them while they were wrongdoers﴾ [al-Ankabut: 14], and similar verses. And such as His saying about the people of Hud: ﴿When We sent upon them the barren wind﴾ and the verse [al-Dhariyat: 41], and similar verses. And such as His saying about the people of Salih: ﴿And the cry seized those who did wrong﴾ and the verse [Hud: 67], and similar verses. And such as His saying about the people of Lut: ﴿So We made its highest part its lowest﴾ and the verse [15], and similar verses. And such as His saying about the people of Shu'ayb: ﴿So they denied him, and the punishment of the Day of the Canopy seized them. Indeed, it was the punishment of a tremendous day﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 189], and similar verses.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 3, verse 13:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿There has already been a sign for you in the two armies which met⁠﴾ [Al 'Imran: 13], the verse. In this noble verse He mentions that the battle of Badr is a sign (āyah), i.e., a proof (ʿalāmah) of the truth of the religion of Islam, for had it not been the truth, the small, weak company that held fast to it would not have overcome the large, strong company that did not hold fast to it.

In another place He explicitly states that the battle of Badr is a clear evidence (bayyinah), i.e., there is no confusion about the truth in its presence, and that is in His saying: ﴿So that he who perished might perish by clear evidence and he who lived might live by clear evidence⁠﴾ [Al-Anfal: 42].

He also explicitly states that the battle of Badr is a criterion (furqān) that distinguishes between truth and falsehood, and that is His saying: ﴿And We sent down upon Our servant on the Day of the Criterion⁠﴾ [Al-Anfal: 41], the verse.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 3, verse 14:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And horses branded [or: marked], and cattle﴾, He did not specify here how many of the kinds fall under the term al-an'am (cattle).

However, He has specified in other places that they are eight kinds: the camel (al-jamal), the she-camel (al-naqah), the bull (al-thawr), the cow (al-baqarah), the ram (al-kabsh), the ewe (al-na'jah), the he-goat (al-tays), and the she-goat (al-anzah), as in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And of the cattle are those for burden and those for flesh﴾ [al-An'am: 142]. Then He specified al-an'am in His saying: ﴿Eight pairs: of the sheep two, and of the goats two﴾ [al-An'am: 143], meaning the ram and the ewe; ﴿and of the goats two﴾, meaning the he-goat and the she-goat; up to His saying: ﴿and of the camels two﴾ [al-An'am: 144], meaning the camel and the she-camel; ﴿and of the cattle two﴾, meaning the bull and the cow. These eight are the ones intended by His saying: ﴿And He sent down for you of the cattle eight pairs﴾ [al-Zumar: 6], and they are the ones indicated by His saying: ﴿Originator of the heavens and the earth; He made for you from yourselves mates, and of the cattle mates﴾ (p-199) [al-Shura: 11].

Note:

The Arabs may sometimes apply the word al-ni'am specifically to camels. From this is His saying ﷺ: "from the red camels of al-ni'am," meaning camels (ﷺ). And the saying of Hassan (may Allah be pleased with him), in the wafir meter:

"There was never cease of company in its pastures, a ni'am (camels) and sheep (shah)."

That is: camels and sheep.

The author said in (Dafʿ Īhām al-Iḍtirāb ʿan Āyāt al-Kitāb):

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Let not the believers take the disbelievers as allies instead of the believers﴾, and so on.

(p-230) This noble verse gives the impression that taking disbelievers as allies is permissible if it is not "instead of the believers," on the basis of His words: ﴿instead of the believers﴾.

Other verses have come that indicate the prohibition of taking them as allies absolutely, such as His exalted saying: ﴿And do not take from them an ally or a helper﴾ [al-Nisa: 89], and His saying: ﴿Do not take as allies those who have taken your religion as a mockery and a game, from among those who were given the Scripture before you, and the disbelievers﴾, and so on [al-Ma'idah: 57].

The answer to this is that His saying ﴿instead of the believers﴾ has no mafhum (implied meaning by contrast).

It has been established in the science of usul al-fiqh (principles of jurisprudence) that dalil al-khitab (the indication of discourse), which is mafhum al-mukhalafah (implication by contrast), has impediments that prevent it from being considered. Among them is that the specification of the stated text by mention is for the sake of its conformity with the actual situation, as in this verse, because it was revealed concerning a people who allied themselves with the Jews instead of the believers. So it was revealed forbidding the situation that actually occurred, without intending to restrict the prohibition to it. Rather, allying with disbelievers is absolutely forbidden. And Allah, exalted is He, knows best.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 3, verse 31:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: If you should love Allah, then follow me; Allah will love you﴾ — the verse. In this noble verse, Allah the Exalted has declared that following His Prophet necessitates the love of Allah, mighty and exalted, for the one who follows. This indicates that obeying His Messenger ﷺ is the very same as obeying Allah, exalted is He. He stated this meaning explicitly in His saying: ﴿Whoever obeys the Messenger has obeyed Allah﴾ [An-Nisa: 80], and He said: ﴿And whatever the Messenger gives you, take it; and what he forbids you, refrain from﴾ [Al-Hashr: 7].

Admonition:

From this noble verse it is derived that the sign of true love for Allah and His Messenger ﷺ is following him ﷺ. Whoever opposes him while claiming to love him is a liar and a fabricator, for if he truly loved him he would obey him. It is well known among the common people that love brings about obedience, and from this is the saying of the poet (metre: al-Kamil):

*If your love were truthful, you would obey him,*
*for the lover is obedient to the one he loves.*

And the saying of Ibn Abi Rabi'ah al-Makhzumi (metre: al-Mutaqarib):

*And one who, if he forbade me from his love,*
*from water while I was thirsty, I would not drink.*

And well has one said (metre: al-Basit):

*She said, when she asked about the state of her lover,*
*"By Allah, describe him, neither exaggerating nor diminishing."*

*I said: Even if he were at the point of death from thirst,*
*and you said, "Stop from approaching the water," he would not approach it.*

The author said in (*Repelling the Appearance of Inconsistency from the Verses of the Book*):

The Exalted said: ﴿There Zechariah called upon his Lord, saying, "My Lord, grant me from Yourself good offspring"﴾, the verse.

This verse indicates that Zechariah, upon him and our Prophet be prayers and peace, had no doubt about the power of Allah to grant him a child despite the old age he had reached. Yet another verse appears to indicate the opposite, namely the Exalted's words: ﴿He said, "My Lord, how can I have a son when old age has overtaken me and my wife is barren?"﴾, the verse [Ali 'Imran: 40].

The answer to this is given in several points:

The first: What Ibn Jarir (al-Tabari) related from Ikrimah and al-Suddi, that when the angels called to Zechariah while he was standing and praying in the sanctuary, saying that Allah gives him good news of Yahya, Satan said to him, "This is not the call of the angels; it is the call of Satan." So doubt entered Zechariah that the call was from Satan. At that doubt, which arose from Satan's whisperings and before he had become certain that it was from Allah, he said: ﴿How can I have a son?﴾ For this reason he asked Allah for a sign concerning it, saying: ﴿My Lord, appoint for me a sign﴾, the verse [Ali 'Imran: 41].

The second: His question was an interrogative (istifham) of seeking information and inquiry, because he did not know whether Allah would bring him a child from his aged wife, or would command him to marry a young woman, or would return them both to youth.

The third: It was an interrogative of magnification and wonder at the perfect power of the Exalted Allah. And Allah knows best.

(p. 231)

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 3, verse 40:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He said, "My Lord, how can I have a son when old age has already overtaken me?"﴾ He did not specify here the degree to which old age had reached him, but He specified in Surat Maryam that he had reached extreme old age ('itiyyan). This is in His saying, exalted is He, about him: ﴿And I have indeed reached extreme old age﴾ [Maryam: 8]. Al-'Itiyy (extreme old age) means dryness and brittleness in the joints and bones due to the severity of old age.

Ibn Jarir (al-Tabari) said in his Tafsir: Everything that has reached its limit in old age, corruption, or disbelief is 'ati (one who has become extremely old or extremely rebellious), and 'asi. His saying, exalted is He, about Zakariyya: ﴿My wife is barren﴾ [Maryam: 8], He did not specify here whether she was like this during her youth, but He specified in Surat Maryam that she was like this before her old age, by His saying about him: ﴿And my wife has been barren,﴾ and so on, to the end of the verse.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He said, "Your sign is that you will not speak to the people for three"﴾. He did not specify whether the one preventing him from speaking to people was a muteness that had come upon him, or an affliction that hindered him from it, or whether there was no preventer for him except Allah, while he was healthy and had no illness.

However, in the surah of "Maryam" he made clear that there was no harm upon him, and that the cessation of his speech was not due to muteness or sickness. This is in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He said, "Your sign is that you will not speak to the people for three nights, while sound"﴾ [Maryam: 10]. For His saying "sawiyyan" (sound, whole) is a ḥāl (circumstantial accusative) referring to the doer of "tukallima" (you speak). It indicates that the cessation of speech was by way of a miracle and a breaking of custom, not due to the tongue being seized by an illness. That is, it would be impossible for you to speak to them, and you would not be able to do so, while you are of sound creation and whole limbs, with no defect of muteness or dumbness in you. This is the view held by the majority of scholars (al-jumhur). It is supported by His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And remember your Lord much and glorify [Him] in the evening and the morning﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 41].

It is related from Ibn ʿAbbās that "sawiyyan" refers back to the nights, meaning complete and even (kāmilāt mustawiyāt), so that it is an attribute of "three" (ṯalāth). According to this view, this verse does not clarify the verse of Āl ʿImrān.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 3, verse 45:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿When the angels said, "O Mary, indeed Allah gives you good tidings of a word from Him"﴾ and so on. Here He did not specify what this word was that was applied to Isa, because it is the cause of his existence, by way of applying the name of the cause while intending its effect (ithlaq al-sabab wa-iradat musabbabihi, i.e., using the cause to mean what it produces). However, He clarified in another place that it is the utterance "Be," and that is in His saying: ﴿Indeed, the likeness of Isa before Allah is like the likeness of Adam; He created him from dust, then said to him, "Be," and he was﴾ [Al 'Imran: 59]. It has been said that the "word" is the angels' glad tidings to her that she would bear him, and this is the view preferred by Ibn Jarir. The first view is the opinion of the majority (al-jumhur).

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 3, verse 46:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And he will speak to the people in the cradle﴾, he did not specify here what he spoke to them in the cradle. However, he specified it in surah "Maryam" with His saying: ﴿So she pointed to him. They said, "How can we speak to one who is in the cradle, a child?" He said, "Indeed, I am the servant of Allah. He has given me the Scripture and made me a prophet. And He has made me blessed wherever I am, and has enjoined upon me prayer and zakah as long as I remain alive. And [He has made me] dutiful to my mother, and He has not made me a除 tyrant or defiant. And peace is upon me the day I was born, and the day I will die, and the day I will be resurrected alive."﴾ [Maryam: 29–33].

(p-201) His saying, exalted is He: ﴿She said: "My Lord, how can I have a child when no man has touched me?"﴾ In this verse He alludes to the story of her conceiving Jesus. Its details are set out in Surah "Maryam" with His saying: ﴿And mention in the Book Maryam, when she withdrew from her family to a place toward the east﴾, ﴿and she took a screen apart from them﴾ — the verse [Maryam 19:16–17] — and so on to the end of the story. He explained the breathing (al-nafkh) into her in Surah "al-Tahrim" and "al-Anbiya'", expressing in al-Tahrim with the breathing into her private part (farj), and in "al-Anbiya'" with the breathing into her.

The author said, in (Dafʿ Ihtimam al-Idtirab ʿan Ayat al-Kitab):

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, I create for you from clay [something] like the form of a bird⦆ — the verse.

The apparent meaning of this verse may give the impression that some created beings might create other beings. A similar example is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And you invent a falsehood⦆ — the verse [al-ʿAnkabut: 17].

Other verses have come which show that Allah is the Creator of everything, such as His saying: ﴿Indeed, We created everything by measure⦆ [al-Qamar: 49], and His saying: ﴿Allah is the Creator of all things, and He is, over all things, Disposer of affairs⦆ [al-Zumar: 62], along with other verses.

The answer is clear: the meaning of ʿIsa's "creating" from clay something like the form of a bird is that he took a portion of clay and shaped it into the form — that is, the figure — of a bird. The intended meaning is not true creation, because Allah alone is unique in that, majestic and exalted is He. As for His saying: ﴿And you invent a falsehood⦆, its meaning is "you lie." So there is no contradiction between the verses, as is evident.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 3, verse 52:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So when Jesus sensed disbelief from them, he said, "Who are my helpers for Allah?" The disciples (al-Hawariyyun) said, "We are helpers of Allah"﴾ — the verse. Here he did not explain the wisdom in mentioning the story of the disciples with Jesus. However, he explained in Surah "al-Saff" that the wisdom in mentioning their story is that the Ummah of Muhammad (ﷺ) might emulate them in supporting Allah and His religion. This is in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿O you who have believed, be helpers of Allah, as Jesus, son of Mary, said to the disciples, "Who are my helpers for Allah?"﴾ — the verse [61:14].

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 3, verse 54:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And they schemed, and Allah schemed, and Allah is the best of schemers﴾. Here he did not specify the scheme of the Jews against Jesus, nor the scheme of Allah against the Jews. However, He made clear in another place that their scheme against him was their attempt to kill him, and that is in His saying: ﴿And their saying, "Indeed, we killed the Messiah, Jesus, son of Mary, the Messenger of Allah"﴾ [al-Nisa': 157-158]. He also made clear that His scheme against them was His casting the likeness onto someone other than Jesus and His rescuing Jesus, peace be upon him and upon our Prophet, and that is in His saying: ﴿And they did not kill him, nor did they crucify him, but it was made to appear so to them﴾ [al-Nisa': 157], and His saying: ﴿And they did not kill him for certain. Rather, Allah raised him to Himself﴾ [al-Nisa': 157-158].

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 3, verse 55:

The words of the Exalted: ﴿When Allah said: "O Jesus, I will take you in death (mutawaffika)..."﴾, the verse.

Some scholars said: meaning, I will save you and raise you to Me during that sleep. This interpretation finds support in the verses in which the word for death (wafah) is applied to sleep, such as His saying: ﴿It is He who takes you back [to Himself] at night...﴾, the verse [al-An'am: 60], and His saying: ﴿Allah takes the souls at the time of their death, and those that do not die during their sleep﴾ [al-Zumar: 42].

⁕ ⁕ ⁕

The author said in (Daf' Iham al-Idtirab 'an Ayat al-Kitab):

The words of the Exalted: ﴿When Allah said: "O Jesus, I will take you in death and raise you to Me"﴾, the verse.

From the apparent meaning of this noble verse, one may imagine that Jesus, upon him and upon our Prophet be prayers and peace, has died.

Some other verses have come that indicate otherwise, such as His saying: ﴿They did not kill him, nor did they crucify him, but it was made to appear so to them﴾ [al-Nisa: 157], and His saying: ﴿And there is none of the People of the Book but will surely believe in him before his death﴾, the verse [al-Nisa: 159].

In accordance with what Ibn 'Abbas explained it in one of the two narrations, and Abu Malik, al-Hasan, Qatadah, Ibn ... and Abu Hurayrah; and the mutawatir hadiths confirm its truth. Ibn Jarir chose it, and Ibn Kathir affirmed it as the truth, that His saying: ﴿before his death﴾ means before the death of Jesus, upon him and upon our Prophet be prayers and peace.

The answer to this is in three aspects:

The first: His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿mutawaffika﴾ does not specify the time, nor does it indicate that it has already occurred, though He will certainly cause him to die at some point; but there is no evidence that this day has already passed. As for its coordination (ʿatf) of "wa rafi'uka" (and raising you) upon "mutawaffika" (I will take you), there is no proof in it, because the majority of the people of the Arabic language agree that the conjunction "wa" (and) does not necessitate sequence (tartib) or simultaneity (jam'), but only indicates general association (tashrik).

Al-Sirafi and al-Suhayli claimed a consensus of the grammarians on this, and most attributed it to the verifiers (al-muhaqqiqin), and it is the truth. This is in contrast to what Qutrub, al-Farra', Tha'lab, Abu 'Umar, al-Zahid, Hisham and al-Shafi'i said, that it indicates sequence due to its frequent use in that sense.

Al-Sirafi denied the authenticity of this view from al-Farra' and said: I did not find it in his book.

Wali al-Din said: Our companions denied attributing this view to al-Shafi'i; it was reported from him by the author of al-Diya' al-Lami'.

As for his saying ﷺ: "Begin with what Allah began with" — meaning al-Safa — there is no evidence in it that "wa" necessitates sequence. The explanation of this is what al-Fihri said, as mentioned by the author of al-Diya' al-Lami': just as it does not necessitate sequence or simultaneity, likewise it does not necessitate prohibition of either of them. Coordination by it may occur while intending priority for the first item, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, al-Safa and al-Marwah are among the symbols of Allah﴾, the verse [al-Baqarah: 158], based on the aforementioned hadith. And the coordinated item may be in sequence, as in the saying of Hassan:

"You satirized Muhammad, and I answered on his behalf"

according to the narration with "wa". And it may intend simultaneity, as in His saying: ﴿So We saved him and the companions of the ship﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 15], and His saying: ﴿And the sun and the moon are joined﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 9]. But it is not to be taken as indicating sequence or simultaneity except with a separate evidence.

The second aspect: the meaning of "mutawaffika" is: causing you to sleep (munimuka), "and raising you to Me", that is, during that sleep.

The Qur'an has applied the word for death (wafah) to sleep in His saying: ﴿It is He who takes you back at night, and knows what you have committed by day﴾ [al-An'am: 60], and His saying: ﴿Allah takes the souls at the time of their death, and those that do not die during their sleep﴾ [al-Zumar: 42].

Ibn Kathir attributed this view to the majority, and cited as evidence the two aforementioned verses and His saying ﷺ: "Praise be to Allah who gave us life after He had caused us to die..." — the hadith.

The third aspect: "mutawaffika" is an active participle of tawaffahu, meaning he received it and took it to himself; from this is the saying: "So-and-so received his debt (tawaffa daynahu)," meaning he took it to himself. So the meaning of "mutawaffika" according to this view is: "the one who will take you from them to Me alive."

This view is the choice of Ibn Jarir. As for reconciling it by saying that He caused him to die for hours or days and then revived him, this is apparently from the Isra'iliyyat, and the Prophet ﷺ forbade either affirming or denying them.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 3, verse 65:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿O People of the Scripture, why do you argue about Abraham?﴾ Here He did not specify what the basis of their argument about Abraham was. However, He clarified in another place that their argument concerning Abraham was the claim of the Jews that he was a Jew, and the claim of the Christians that he was a Christian. This is in His saying: ﴿Or do you say that Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, and the Tribes were Jews or Christians? Say: Are you more knowing or is Allah?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 140]. (p-202) He alluded to this here in His saying: ﴿And Allah knows, while you do not know.﴾ ﴿Abraham was neither a Jew nor a Christian﴾, and the verse [Ali 'Imran: 66-67].

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 3, verse 67:

The author said in (Daf' Iham al-Idtirab 'an Ayat al-Kitab):

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Abraham was neither a Jew nor a Christian, but he was a true monotheist (hanif), a Muslim. And he was not of the polytheists.﴾ and so on.

This noble verse and its like in the Qur'an indicate that Abraham, upon him and upon our Prophet be prayers and peace, was never a polytheist at any time, because the negation of the past state in His saying ﴿and he was not of the polytheists﴾ indicates that the negation encompasses the whole of the past time, as His exalted saying indicates: ﴿And We gave Abraham his guidance before, [and We were Knowing of him]﴾ [al-Anbiya': 51].

In another place there occurs what seems to contradict this, namely His saying: ﴿So when the night covered him, he saw a star. He said, "This is my lord." But when it set, he said, "I like not those that set."﴾ ﴿Then when he saw the moon rising, he said, "This is my lord." But when it set, he said, "Unless my Lord guides me, I will surely be among the people who are astray."﴾ ﴿Then when he saw the sun rising, he said, "This is my lord; this is greater." But when it set, he said, "O my people, indeed I am free from what you associate."﴾ and so on [al-An'am: 76-78].

Whoever supposes the lordship of other than Allah is a polytheist with respect to Allah, as His exalted saying concerning the disbelievers indicates: ﴿And those who call upon other than Allah as partners follow not [their] partners; they follow not except assumption, and they are not but guessing﴾ [Yunus: 66].

The answer to this is in two respects. The first: he was a debater (munazir), not an examiner (nazir), and his intent was dialectical concession (al-taslim al-jadali), i.e., "This is my lord" according to your false claim. The debater may concede a false premise dialectically in order to silence his opponent thereby.

For if Abraham had said to them at the outset, "The star is created and cannot be a lord," they would have said to him, "You lie; rather the star is a lord." Among what indicates that he was a debater and not an examiner is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And his people argued with him﴾ [al-An'am: 80].

This respect is the more apparent. As for what Ibn Jarir cited to show that he was not a debater, from His saying, exalted is He:

(p-234) ﴿Unless my Lord guides me, I will surely be among the people who are astray﴾ [al-An'am: 77].

There is no proof in it with verification, because the messengers say the like of this out of humility and to show their turning to Allah, as in the saying of Abraham: ﴿And keep me and my sons away from worshipping idols﴾ [Ibrahim: 35], and his saying, together with Isma'il: ﴿Our Lord, make us Muslims [submitting] to You﴾ [al-Baqarah: 128].

The second respect: the speech is according to the omission of the interrogative hamza, i.e., "Is this my lord?" It is established in the science of grammar (ilm al-nahw) that omitting the interrogative hamza when the context indicates it is permissible, and according to al-Akhfash it is analogical (qiyasi), both with "am" and without it, whether the answer is mentioned or not. Among its examples without "am" and without mention of the answer is the saying of al-Kumayt:

"I was delighted, and not with longing for the fair ones do I delight, nor is it playfulness from me, and does the one with gray hair play?"

i.e., "Or does the one with gray hair play?" And the saying of Abu Khirash al-Hudhali, whose name is Khuwaylid:

"They pushed me back and said, 'O Khuwaylid, do not be alarmed,' so I said, while I denied the faces, 'They are they.'"

i.e., "Are they they?" as is the correct view, and al-Alusi affirmed it in his tafsir, and Ibn Jarir mentioned it from a group; and his saying "and I denied the faces" indicates it.

Among its examples without "am" but with the answer mentioned is the saying of Umar ibn Abi Rabi'ah al-Makhzumi:

"Then they said, 'Do you love her?' I said, abruptly, 'as many as the stars, the pebbles and the dust.'"

i.e., "Do you love her?" according to the correct view. With "am" it is very common. Among its examples is the saying of al-Aswad ibn Ya'fur al-Tamimi, which Sibawayh recited for this purpose:

"By your life, I do not know, though I am knowledgeable, whether Shu'ayth ibn Sahm or Shu'ayth ibn Minqar [is meant]."

i.e., "Is it Shu'ayth ibn Sahm?" And the saying of Ibn Abi Rabi'ah al-Makhzumi:

"There appeared to me from her a wrist, when she threw [the pebbles], and a dyed palm adorned with fingers."

"By God, I do not know, and I am a counter, whether I threw the pebbles with seven or with eight."

i.e., "With seven?" And the saying of al-Akhtal:

"Did your eye deceive you, or did you see, in Wasit, at the dim dawn of darkness, from al-Rabab, a phantom?"

(p-235) i.e., "Did your eye deceive you?" as Sibawayh explicitly stated the permissibility of this in the verse of al-Akhtal, although he differed from al-Khalil, who held that "kadhabatka" is a declarative form and that "am" means "bal." According to al-Khalil's view there is in the verse a kind of rhetorical figure of meaning, called al-ruju' (return) by the rhetoricians.

And the saying of al-Khansa':

"A speck in your two eyes, or is it the eye that is blind? Or has the abode been emptied when its people left it desolate?"

i.e., "Is it a speck in your eyes?" And the saying of Uhayhah ibn al-Julah al-Ansari:

"You do not know, even if you drive a young camel for another, or whether the young camel will be yours."

i.e., "For another?" And the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

"Do you depart from the tribe, or hasten in the morning? What is upon you that you should wait?"

i.e., "Do you depart?"

According to this view, the indicator of the omitted interrogative is the high station of Abraham above the supposition of the lordship of other than Allah, and the Qur'an's testimony to his innocence of that. The verse on this view resembles the reading of Ibn Muhaysin: ﴿It is the same for them whether you warn them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 6]. Its parallel on this view is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then if you die, will they be the immortals?﴾ [al-Anbiya': 34], i.e., "Will they be the immortals?"

And His saying: ﴿And this is a favor by which you reproach me﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 22], according to one of the two views, and His saying: ﴿But he has not attempted the steep path﴾ [al-Balad: 11], according to one of the two views.

Whatever some scholars have mentioned other than these two respects returns to them, such as the view of supposing an implied "saying," i.e., the disbelievers say "This is my lord," for it returns to the first respect.

As for what Ibn Ishaq mentioned and what al-Tabari Ibn Jarir chose, transmitting it from Ibn 'Abbas, that Abraham was an examiner supposing the lordship of the star, it is manifestly weak, because the texts of the Qur'an reject it:

• such as His saying: ﴿But he was neither a Jew nor a Christian, but he was a true monotheist, a Muslim, and he was not of the polytheists﴾ [Al 'Imran: 67].

• and His exalted saying: ﴿Then We revealed to you, [O Muhammad], to follow the religion of Abraham, inclining toward truth; and he was not of the polytheists﴾ [al-Nahl: 123],

• and His saying: ﴿And We had certainly given Abraham his guidance before﴾ [al-Anbiya': 51].

(p-236)

The verifier Ibn Kathir, in his tafsir, has explained the rejection of what Ibn Jarir mentioned by these Qur'anic texts and their like, and by the hadiths indicating their meaning, such as his saying ﷺ: "Every child is born upon the fitrah," the hadith.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 3, verse 90 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve after their belief and then increase in disbelief - their repentance will never be accepted﴾.

Some scholars said: It means that if they delay repentance until the arrival of death, then repent at that time. This interpretation is supported by His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And repentance is not [accepted] from those who continue to do evil deeds until, when death approaches one of them, he says, "Indeed, I have now repented," nor from those who die while they are disbelievers﴾ [An-Nisa': 18]. It is established in the principles of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh) that the absolute (mutlaq) is to be understood in light of the qualified (muqayyad), especially when the ruling and the cause are the same, as is the case here.

Another group of scholars said: The meaning of "their repentance will never be accepted" is that they will not be granted success in repentance until it is accepted from them. This is supported by His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, those who believed, then disbelieved, then believed, then disbelieved, then increased in disbelief - Allah will never forgive them, nor will He guide them to a way﴾ [An-Nisa': 137]. Their not being forgiven is because of their not being guided to the way that forgives its follower. A parallel to this is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Allah will never forgive them, nor will He guide them to any path, ﴿except the path of Hell﴾﴾ [An-Nisa': 168-169].

⁕ ⁕ ⁕

The author said in (Daf' Iham al-Idtirab 'an Ayat al-Kitab):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve after their belief and then increase in disbelief - their repentance will never be accepted, and those are the ones who are astray﴾.

This noble verse indicates that apostates who, after their belief, increase in disbelief, will not have their repentance accepted by Allah if they repent, because He expressed it with "lan" (never), which denotes negation of the action in the future. However, there are other verses indicating that Allah accepts the repentance of every penitent before the arrival of death and before the sun rises from its west, such as:

• His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Say to those who disbelieve: If they desist, they will be forgiven what has already passed﴾ [Al-Anfal: 38],

• and His saying: ﴿And it is He who accepts repentance from His servants﴾ [Ash-Shura: 25],

• and His saying: ﴿The day when some of the signs of your Lord come, no soul will benefit from its belief unless it had believed before﴾ [Al-An'am: 158].

Its implication indicates that repentance before the coming of some of the signs is accepted from every penitent. Allah has explicitly included apostates among those whose repentance is accepted, immediately before this verse, in His saying: ﴿How will Allah guide a people who disbelieved after their belief and having testified that the Messenger is true...﴾ up to His saying: ﴿except for those who repent after that and reform, for indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [Aal 'Imran: 86-89].

So the exception in His saying ﴿except those who repent﴾ refers to the apostates after belief who deserve punishment and curse if they do not repent. This is also supported by His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And whoever of you reverts from his religion and dies while he is a disbeliever﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 217], the verse, because its implication is that if he repents before death, his repentance is accepted absolutely.

The answer comes in four ways:

First: This is the view preferred by Ibn Jarir, which he transmitted from Rufay' Abu al-'Aliyah: the meaning is: Indeed, those who disbelieved among the Jews in Muhammad (ﷺ) after their belief in him before his mission, then increased in disbelief through the sins they committed in their disbelief - their repentance will never be accepted for their sins which they committed in their disbelief until they repent from their disbelief. This interpretation is supported by His saying: ﴿and those are the ones who are astray﴾, because it indicates that their repentance while they remain committed to error is not accepted, which is evident.

Second: This is the closest of them in my view: that His saying ﴿their repentance will never be accepted﴾ means when they repent at the arrival of death. Two matters support this interpretation:

The first: that He, may He be exalted, explained in other places that the disbeliever whose repentance is not accepted is the one who persists in disbelief until death comes upon him and then repents at that time, as in His saying: ﴿And repentance is not [accepted] from those who continue to do evil deeds until, when death approaches one of them, he says, "Indeed, I have now repented," nor from those who die while they are disbelievers﴾ [An-Nisa': 18].

Thus the penitent at the arrival of death and the one who dies in his disbelief are made equal.

And His saying: ﴿And their belief was not beneficial to them when they saw Our punishment﴾, the verse [Ghafir: 85].

And His saying about Pharaoh: ﴿Now? And you had disobeyed before and were among the corrupters﴾ [Yunus: 91].

So the unrestricted statement in this verse is restricted by the condition of delaying repentance until the arrival of death, due to the obligation to understand the absolute in light of the qualified, as is established in the principles.

The second: He, may He be exalted, indicated this by His saying: ﴿then increased in disbelief﴾, for it indicates that they did not repent at the time when repentance would benefit. Ibn Jarir transmitted this second view, which is the restriction by the arrival of death, from al-Hasan, Qatadah, 'Ata' al-Khurasani and al-Suddi.

Third: that the meaning of ﴿their repentance will never be accepted﴾ is their first belief, because it was nullified by apostasy after it. Ibn Jarir transmitted this view from Ibn Jurayj, and the weakness of this view and its distance from the apparent meaning of the Qur'an is not hidden.

Fourth: that what is intended by His saying ﴿their repentance will never be accepted﴾ is that they will not be granted success in sincere repentance (tawbah nasuhah) until it is accepted from them. This interpretation is supported by His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who believed, then disbelieved, then believed, then disbelieved, then increased in disbelief - Allah will never forgive them, nor will He guide them to a way﴾ [An-Nisa': 137].

His saying: ﴿nor will He guide them to a way﴾ indicates that His not forgiving them is due to their not being granted success in repentance and guidance.

Like His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieved and wronged - Allah will never forgive them, nor will He guide them to a path, ﴿except the path of Hell﴾﴾ [An-Nisa': 168].

(p-238) And like His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, those upon whom the word of your Lord has been justified will not believe﴾, the verse [Yunus: 96].

The parallel of the verse according to this view is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So the intercession of the interceders will not benefit them﴾ [Al-Muddaththir: 48], meaning there is no intercession for them at all so that it could benefit them; and His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And whoever invokes along with Allah another deity for which he has no proof﴾, the verse [Al-Mu'minun: 117], because the other deity cannot exist at all, so that a proof could be established for it or not established for it.

The one who restricts it (may Allah pardon him) says: This last view is well known among the logicians (nuzzar) by their saying: "The negative proposition does not entail the existence of the subject." Its clarification is that a negative proposition, in their view, is true in two situations, because what is intended by it is the non-attribution of the predicate to the subject, and this non-attribution is realized in two situations:

The first: that the subject exists but the predicate is negated from it, as in your saying: "Man is not a stone," so man exists and stone-ness is negated from him.

The second: that the subject is non-existent from its origin, because when it does not exist, the non-attribution of the existential predicate is realized, since non-existence cannot be attributed with existence, as in your saying: "There is no equal to Allah who deserves worship," for the subject which is the equal is not impossible from its origin; and when its non-existence is established, the negation of its attribution with the deserving of worship is necessarily established. This type is one of the styles of the Arabic language, and among its evidences is the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

"Over a well-trodden road whose signposts are not followed, when the Nabataean wind blows against it and it rumbles."

Because the meaning is: over a well-trodden road that has no signpost at all by which one could be guided.

And the saying of another:

"Its terrors do not frighten the hare, and you do not see the lizard burrowing in it."

Because he describes a desert in which there are no hares or lizards, so that its terrors could frighten the hare, or the lizard could burrow in it, i.e., enter the hole or take it as a home. I have clarified the matter that a negative proposition does not require the existence of the subject in my poem on logic, in the section on the deviation of the figures (inhiraf al-suwar), and I also clarified in it, in the section on the obtaining and the alteration (al-tahsil wal-'udul), that among affirmative propositions there are some that do not require the existence of the subject, such as: "A sea of mercury is possible," and "the impossible is non-existent"; for these are two affirmative propositions and the subject of each of them is non-existent. There I verified the detailed discussion of what requires the existence of the subject and what does not require it.

What we have established, that the apostate who repents has his repentance accepted even after repeating apostasy three times or more, is not inconsistent with what a group of the four imams and others said, and it is related from 'Ali and Ibn 'Abbas: that the apostate who repeats this is to be killed and his repentance is not accepted. Some of them used this verse as evidence for that. This disagreement concerns the realization of the cause (tahqiq al-manat), while both sides agree on the underlying cause (asl al-manat). Its clarification: the manat is the place of hanging (nawt), which is suspension, and from it is the saying of Hassan, may Allah be pleased with him:

"You are an illegitimate child attached within the family of Hashim, as the single cup is hung behind the rider."

What is meant by it is the place where the ruling is suspended, which is the 'illah (effective cause). Thus manat and 'illah are technically synonymous, except that the expression "manat" has become predominant for the fifth method of establishing the 'illah, which is suitability and relevance (munasabah wal-ihalah), as it is called takhrij al-manat (extraction of the cause); and likewise in the ninth method, which is tanqih al-manat (refinement of the cause). Takhrij al-manat is the extraction of the cause by the method of suitability and relevance, and tanqih al-manat is the purification and refinement of the cause so that nothing suitable for it is excluded and nothing unsuitable for it is included, as is known in its proper place. As for tahqiq al-manat, which is the purpose here, it is that the ground of the ruling is agreed upon between the two disputants, but one of them says it exists in this branch, and the other says it does not.

Its example is the disagreement about the cutting of the hand of the grave-robber (nabbash). Abu Hanifah, may Allah have mercy on him, agrees with the majority that theft is the cause of amputation, but he says the cause has not been realized in the grave-robber, because he is not a thief; rather he is one who takes property that is exposed to loss, like one who picks up something from outside a protected place. When you have understood this, know that the intention of those who say his repentance is not accepted is that his actions indicate the corruption of his intention and the corruption of his belief, and that he is not a penitent in falsehood with sincere repentance. They agree with the sincere repentance as the cause of acceptance, as we have mentioned, but they say the actions of this wicked one show that the cause has not been realized.

Hence scholars differed concerning the repentance of the zindiq (one who conceals disbelief), that is, one who hides disbelief. Some say his repentance is not accepted, some say it is accepted, and some distinguish between his coming in repentance before being discovered and his being discovered in his hypocrisy before repenting, as is known in the branches of the four schools of law. Those who say he is to be killed and his repentance is not accepted hold that his hidden falsehood is evidence that his repentance is mere dissimulation (taqiyyah), not reality. They used as evidence His saying: ﴿except those who repent and reform﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 160].

(p-240) They said: reformation is a condition, and the zindiq is not known to have reformed, because corruption came only from what he concealed; so when he is discovered and shows abandonment, he remains inwardly as he was. What appears is that the evidences of those who say his repentance is accepted absolutely are clearer and stronger, such as the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) to Usamah, may Allah be pleased with him: "Why did you not split open his heart?" And his saying to the one who whispered to him about killing a man, and he said: "Does he not pray?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Those are the ones I have been forbidden to kill." And his saying to Khalid when he asked his permission to kill the one who denied the distribution: "I have not been commanded to search into the hearts of people." These hadiths are in the Sahih. What also indicates this is the consensus that the rulings of this world are based on the outward, and Allah takes charge of the hidden matters.

He, may He be exalted, has explicitly stated that false oaths are a shield for the hypocrites in worldly rulings, in His saying: ﴿They have taken their oaths as a shield﴾ [Al-Mujadilah: 16],

• and His saying: ﴿They will swear to you by Allah when you return to them, that you may leave them alone. So leave them alone; indeed they are an abomination﴾ [At-Tawbah: 95].

• and His saying: ﴿And they swear by Allah that they are surely of you, but they are not of you﴾, the verse [At-Tawbah: 56].

And other verses besides these.

As for what some have cited, namely that Ibn Mas'ud killed Ibn al-Nawwaha, the companion of Musaylima, it is answered that he killed him in accordance with the words of the Prophet ﷺ when he came to him as an envoy from Musaylima: "Were it not that envoys are not to be killed, I would have killed you." So Ibn Mas'ud killed him in fulfilment of the Prophet's ﷺ words.

It has been narrated that he killed him for this reason. If it is said: this verse, which indicates that their repentance is not accepted, is more specific than other verses, because it contains the restriction to apostasy and increase in disbelief. Thus the one who repeatedly apostatizes is more specific than the apostate in general, and evidence for the more general does not constitute evidence for the more specific, because the existence of the general does not necessitate the existence of the specific.

The answer is that the Qur'an indicates the acceptance of the repentance of one who repeatedly disbelieves, if he sincerely turns back to Allah. The manner in which the Qur'an indicates this is that He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, those who believe, then disbelieve, then believe, then disbelieve, then increase in disbelief—Allah will never forgive them, nor will He guide them to a way﴾ [an-Nisa: 137].

Then He made clear that the hypocrites are included among them by His saying: ﴿Give good tidings to the hypocrites that for them is a painful punishment﴾ [an-Nisa: 138], and so on.

Although the usuliyyun (scholars of legal theory) have weakened the indication by association (dalalat al-iqtiran), a group of verifying scholars have authenticated it, especially when it is reinforced by a contextual indicator, as is the case here, through His saying: (p-241) ﴿He will never forgive them, nor will He guide them to a way﴾ and ﴿Give good tidings to the hypocrites that for them is a painful punishment﴾. In this there is clear indication that they are included in what is meant by the verse. Indeed, a group of scholars has held that the verse is specifically about them.

When you have verified this, know that Allah, exalted is He, stated explicitly that whoever among the hypocrites sincerely repents, Allah accepts his repentance, by His saying: ﴿Indeed, the hypocrites will be in the lowest level of the Fire, and you will not find for them a helper﴾ ﴿except those who repent, amend, hold fast to Allah, and make their religion sincerely for Allah. Those will be with the believers, and Allah will give the believers a great reward﴾ ﴿Why would Allah punish you if you are grateful and believe? And Allah is ever Appreciative and Knowing﴾ [an-Nisa: 145–147].

Makhshi ibn Himyar, may Allah be pleased with him, was among the hypocrites concerning whom Allah revealed His saying: ﴿And if you asked them, they would surely say, "We were only conversing and playing." Say, "Is it Allah and His verses and His Messenger that you were mocking?"﴾ ﴿Make no excuse; you have disbelieved after your belief﴾ [at-Tawbah: 65–66].

He repented to Allah sincerely, so Allah accepted his repentance, and Allah revealed concerning him: ﴿If We pardon a faction among you, We will punish another faction﴾ [at-Tawbah: 66] and so on.

The conclusion is that those who hold that the repentance of one who repeatedly apostatizes is not accepted mean the worldly rulings, and they do not disagree that if he sincerely repents to Allah, it is accepted from him, because their disagreement lies in the verification of the applicable case (tahqiq al-manat), as has preceded. And knowledge is with Allah, exalted is He.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 3, verse 91:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve and die while they are disbelievers, never will be accepted from any of them the earth filled with gold even if he were to ransom himself with it﴾ — the verse. In this noble verse He states explicitly that on the Day of Resurrection there will not be accepted from any of them the earth filled with gold, even if he offers it as ransom.

And He states explicitly in other places that even if the like of it were added, it would not be accepted from him either.

Such as His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve, if they had all that is in the earth and the like of it with it, to ransom themselves thereby from the punishment of the Day of Resurrection, it would not be accepted from them﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 36]. And He clarified in other places that no ransom will be accepted from them on that Day at all,

such as His saying: ﴿So today no ransom will be taken from you, nor from those who disbelieved﴾ [al-Hadid: 15],

and His saying: ﴿And if they offer every ransom, it will not be taken from them﴾ [al-An'am: 70],

and His saying: ﴿Nor will compensation be accepted from it, nor will intercession benefit it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 123].

Al-'adl (عدل) means the ransom (fida' — redemption payment).

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 3, verse 97:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And whoever disbelieves - indeed, Allah is free of need from the worlds﴾. In this verse He declares explicitly that He is free of need from His creation, and that the disbelief of those among them who disbelieve does not harm Him in any way. He has explained this meaning in many places,

• such as His saying concerning His prophet Musa: ﴿And Musa said, "If you disbelieve, you and whoever is on earth entirely, then indeed Allah is Free of need and Praiseworthy"﴾ [Ibrahim: 8],

• and His saying: ﴿If you disbelieve, then indeed Allah is free of need from you, and He does not approve for His servants disbelief﴾ [az-Zumar: 7],
